slides.title: I/O Hardware Overview
slides.body:
Three Physical Layers
Heading: I/O Hardware Overview
Subheading: Three Physical Layers
Content:
Every device connects to the CPU through three hardware layers that standardise wildly different devices into one interface.
Ports: registers holding device data & status
Buses: shared wires carrying signals between components
Device controllers: hardware managing one device type

Polling: CPU repeatedly checks status register
Busy-waiting wastes CPU cycles until device ready
Interrupt: device signals CPU on completion
CPU works elsewhere until interrupt arrives

Non-blocking call: returns immediately, maybe with partial data

Asynchronous: caller continues, no waiting at all

slides.title: Multiplexing And Async
slides.body:
Select Poll Epoll AIO
Heading: Multiplexing And Async
Subheading: Select Poll Epoll AIO
Content:
Non-blocking multiplexing checks many descriptors at once; true asynchronous I/O uses kernel completion queues instead.
select()/poll(): scan file descriptor set for readiness
epoll (Linux): scalable event notification, avoids full rescans
Signal-driven I/O: kernel sends SIGIO on readiness
io_uring/POSIX aio: kernel completes operation, queues result
Non-blocking multiplexing checks many descriptors at once; true asynchronous I/O uses kernel completion queues instead

slides.title: Choosing I/O Model
slides.body:
Real World Deployments
Heading: Choosing I/O Model
Subheading: Real World Deployments
Content:
Production systems pick an I/O model based on connection scale, latency needs and programming complexity.
Nginx, Node.js: non-blocking event loop with epoll
Database engines: asynchronous I/O via io_uring, less CPU spin
Simple utilities: blocking I/O, code stays straightforward
GUI apps: non-blocking keeps interface responsive
Production systems pick an I/O model based on connection scale, latency needs and programming complexity
